To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mutations of USH1 genes cause primary defects in the sensory cells of the inner ear and retina, and that the molecular pathogenesis is likely to be the same in all three subtypes of USH1.

the USH1 proteins are involved in a signaling pathway that controls the adhesion force at the stereocilia and/or at the level of their junctions to the cuticular plate, whereas the pathogenesis of USh2A is probably different.

mutations of the USH1B (myosin 7A), USH1C (harmonin) and USH1F (cadherin 23) genes are involved in a single pathway, which is probably required for the development and/or maintenance, via adhesion forces, of the hair bundles in the inner ear and the retina.

USH is a complex disorder that involves a number of genes, which may be responsible for the same pathogenic mechanism.
we have identified the genes for three of the four subtypes of Usher syndrome, which have provided new insights into the molecular pathogenesis and pathophysiology of this disorder.

the study of a genetic disease can provide new insights on the molecular mechanisms that control the development of a particular organ.

the study of USH has provided a unique opportunity to investigate how the sensory cells in our ears and eyes function.
